caption_or_description: A lens may be thought of as a set of blocks and prisms: (a) a converging lens and (b) a diverging lens.

Wavefronts travel more slowly in glass than in air. (a) The waves are retarded more through the center of the lens, and convergence results. (b) The waves are retarded more at the edges, and divergence results.
Key features of a converging lens.

The moving patterns of bright and dark areas at the bottom of the pool result from the uneven surface of the water, which behaves like a blanket of undulating lenses. Just as we see the pool bottom shimmering, a fish looking upward at the Sun would see it shimmering too. Because of similar irregularities in the atmosphere, we see the stars twinkle.

caption_or_description: Image formation. (a) No image appears on the wall because rays from all parts of the object overlap all parts of the wall. (b) A single small opening in a barrier prevents overlapping rays from reaching the wall; a dim upside-down image is formed. (c) A lens converges the rays upon the wall without overlapping; more light makes a brighter image.
Thin-lens equation diagram showing object distance, image distance, focal length, and real image.

When an object is near a converging lens (inside its focal point f), the lens acts as a magnifying glass to produce a virtual image. The image appears larger and farther from the lens than the object.
When an object is far from a converging lens (beyond its focal point), a real upside-down image is formed.
A diverging lens forms a virtual, right-side-up image of Jamie and his cat.
